name: Vaasa
title: Vaasa Ship Thickness Gauging: UTM in the Kvarken
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at the Port of Vaasa: hull, ice belt and tank gauging on ro-pax, project cargo and general cargo ships in the Kvarken.
h1: Hull and Tank Thickness Measurement for Ships Calling at Vaasa
intro: Vaasa faces the Kvarken, the narrow, shallow strait where the Gulf of Bothnia pinches between Finland and Sweden. Its port on the island of Vaskiluoto handles the year-round ferry to Umeå, heavy project cargo from the town's energy-technology industry, and general and bulk cargo for Ostrobothnia. Gauging here usually rides on a ferry docking plan, a project loading or a winter check of the ice belt. Each job is staffed by technicians who fly in from India for that ship, as nobody is kept at the port.

highlights.h: The Kvarken ferry and its dockings
highlights.p: The Vaasa–Umeå crossing keeps running through the winter with a single modern ro-pax. Her dockings and off-service days are the only long breaks she gets, so a gauging scope for car deck, tanks and ice belt is prepared well before each one.

highlights.h: Heavy project cargo out of Vaasa
highlights.p: Engines, transformers and other heavy units built in and around Vaasa leave on multipurpose and heavy-lift ships. Loading them takes time and care, which leaves room to gauge tank tops, tween decks and crane pedestal structure before the ship sails.

highlights.h: Shallow fairways and a rising seabed
highlights.p: Narrow channels through skerries and a seabed that slowly rises make bottom contact a real risk for ships working this coast. After any grounding or touch, owners want shell and double-bottom readings to know whether the plating has thinned or been damaged.

port.h: Vaasa, the Kvarken and the ships that use them
p: Vaasa sits on the Finnish shore of the Kvarken, where the Gulf of Bothnia narrows to its tightest point and the water between the Bothnian Sea and the Bay of Bothnia becomes shallow and crowded with islands. The Kvarken Archipelago, together with Sweden's High Coast opposite, is a UNESCO World Heritage site because the land here is still rising after the last ice age, and the shoreline changes visibly within a lifetime. For shipping that means narrow buoyed fairways through the skerries, a seabed that slowly comes up to meet the keel, and dredging to keep the approaches usable. The port itself is on Vaskiluoto, an island just west of the town centre linked to it by bridge, with the passenger terminal and the cargo quays grouped close together.

Traffic at Vaasa is a mix rather than a single trade. The ro-pax Aurora Botnia, run by Wasaline for a company owned jointly by the cities of Vaasa and Umeå, crosses to Holmsund on the Swedish side on a daily timetable and keeps going through the winter, carrying cars, lorries and passengers. Cargo ships bring in and take out general cargo, forest products and dry bulk for the region, while the town's engineering and energy-technology industry ships heavy engines, transformers and power equipment that need multipurpose ships with their own heavy cranes. Most of the ships are small and medium short-sea tonnage under a spread of European flags, and a large share of the regular callers hold a Finnish-Swedish ice class because the port works all year.

The calendar matters more at Vaasa than at most European ports. In a normal winter the Kvarken freezes, drift ice packs into ridges in the narrow strait, and ships rely on icebreaker assistance and on the winter traffic restrictions that set the minimum ice class and size for each Finnish port. Ships on the Vaasa run therefore take their heaviest wear in the ice belt and bow between the first freeze and the spring thaw, and the coating loss shows up as rust streaks along the waterline once the ice has gone. The lighter summer months are when most dockings, repairs and survey work happen, both on the ferry and on the cargo ships. A gauging job planned for Vaasa usually has a seasonal reason: before winter, to confirm the ice belt, or after it, to measure what the ice took.

facilities.h: Where a ship can be gauged at Vaasa
p: Most gauging at Vaasa is done alongside at Vaskiluoto. A cargo ship working general cargo or timber gives a day or more at the quay, enough to measure deck plating, hatch coamings and the ballast tanks the crew has opened and ventilated, and to work through the holds as they are cleared. Project-cargo calls are slower still, because heavy lifts are planned to the hour and the ship often waits for road convoys, so tween decks, tank tops under the stow and crane foundations can be measured in the gaps. The ferry is a different case: her time at the quay between crossings is short, so work aboard her is done on night lay-overs and during off-service days agreed with the operator.

We do not plan full renewal-survey dockings at Vaasa. Ships trading here are usually docked by their owners at repair yards elsewhere in the Baltic, for example Turku Repair Yard at Naantali on Finland's south-west coast. What a Vaasa call offers is the chance to gauge before that docking, so the yard receives a measured steel list rather than an estimate. In winter, ships occasionally wait off the port for an icebreaker or a berth, but boarding a ship in drifting ice is rarely practical, so winter gauging is planned for the quay.
list: Vaskiluoto passenger terminal — the Umeå ro-pax on night lay-overs and off-service days; car deck, void and ice-belt gauging in planned stages
Vaskiluoto cargo quays — general cargo, forest products and dry bulk; hold, hatch coaming and ballast-tank gauging during loading and discharge
Heavy-lift and project cargo berths — multipurpose ships loading engines and transformers; tween deck, tank top and crane pedestal readings between lifts
Lay-by berths in the port — short-sea ships waiting between cargoes; owner's condition or pre-purchase gauging arranged through the agent
Repair yards elsewhere in the Baltic — in-dock verification of readings first taken at Vaasa, when the owner wants the same team at the docking

context.h: Ice classes, land uplift and inspection rules for Vaasa
p: Finland belongs to the Paris MoU, and port state control inspections at Vaasa are carried out by Traficom, the Finnish Transport and Communications Agency, which also issues Finland's ice class regulations. Those regulations link a ship's ice class (IA Super, IA, IB or IC) to the scantlings and engine power it must have, and the winter traffic restrictions decide which ice classes and sizes of ship receive icebreaker assistance into each port. For an owner keeping a ship on the Vaasa trade, the ice class works as a commercial licence, and it depends on ice-belt plating staying within the thickness the class requires. Gauging the ice belt, frames and bow structure before the restrictions tighten each winter is the practical way to know the remaining margin.

The Kvarken ferry runs entirely between Finland and Sweden, so its emissions fall wholly under the EU ETS, which has covered shipping since 2024, and under FuelEU Maritime, in force since 2025. Aurora Botnia burns LNG with battery support, which moves the gauging focus away from scrubber piping and towards the ordinary structure of a hard-working ice-going ferry: car decks, ramps, ice belt and ballast tanks. Cargo ships coming to Vaasa from outside the EU must carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation, and buyers of second-hand ice-class tonnage increasingly ask for IHM status alongside the steel condition.

jobs.p: Vaasa jobs tend to be planned around the ferry calendar, the project-cargo programme and the turn of the seasons. Ferry work is staged across lay-overs and finished before the docking, so the yard knows the steel it must renew. Cargo-ship work is fitted into loading or discharge at Vaskiluoto, with the scope ordered so the most important spaces are measured first in case the ship sails early. Winter brings short-notice requests after ice contact, when an owner needs to know whether a dent or scored shell has lost thickness. Summer brings the planned survey and pre-purchase work, when holds and tanks can be opened and ventilated without the cold getting in the way.
list: Pre-docking gauging of the ro-pax car deck, ballast tanks and ice belt over several lay-overs, so the steel list is fixed before she leaves for the yard
Measuring tween decks, tank tops and crane pedestal structure on a heavy-lift ship loading transformers or engines at Vaskiluoto
Shell and frame gauging in the ice belt after an ice-damage report, with magnetic particle checks on frames and brackets where cracking is suspected
Intermediate-survey gauging of holds and ballast tanks on a short-sea general cargo ship discharging at Vaasa
Pre-purchase condition gauging on a small ice-class cargo ship during a call, with IHM status noted for the buyer

logistics: Vaasa Airport, close to the town, is reached on domestic connections through Helsinki, and the team drives the short distance on to Vaskiluoto. Finland is in the Schengen area, so our technicians travel from India on a Schengen visa, and we start the consular process as soon as the ferry docking or the cargo window is fixed. ISPS gate passes for the cargo quays and the ferry terminal are requested by the ship's agent, and any work aboard the ferry is booked with the operator. In winter we leave a margin for flight disruption and icebreaker delays.

faqs.q: Can you gauge the Vaasa–Umeå ferry without taking her out of service?
faqs.a: Largely, yes. Car-deck plating, voids, tanks the crew can open and the ice belt from inside can be measured during night lay-overs and planned off-service days, a section at a time, with each visit closing off complete areas. External bottom plating and the underwater shell still need the docking. Doing the internal work first means the yard and the surveyor start the docking with most of the readings already on the table.

faqs.q: What does ice do to a ship's steel on the Kvarken route?
faqs.a: Ice strips the coating from the ice belt and bow, and the bare steel then corrodes faster through the summer. Ridged ice in the strait can also dent plating and load frames hard enough to crack brackets and welds. We gauge plating and frames in the ice belt, look for local thinning around dents, and add magnetic particle checks on frame connections where the crew or the surveyor has seen damage.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock at Vaasa for a renewal survey?
faqs.a: We plan renewal-survey dockings for Vaasa ships at repair yards elsewhere in the Baltic, chosen by the owner. What we do at Vaasa is the groundwork: gauging the tanks, holds and decks during an earlier call, so the yard can plan steel renewal from measured figures and book the right number of dock days. The same team can then verify bottom and shell readings once the ship is in dock.

faqs.q: Can holds be gauged while project cargo is being loaded?
faqs.a: Partly. Holds and tween decks can be measured before the stow is built, and the areas under heavy units have to be done first because they disappear once the cargo is lashed. Crane pedestals, deck plating and ballast tanks can be done at any point in the loading. We agree a sequence with the chief officer and the stevedores so readings never hold up a lift.

faqs.q: Is winter a bad time for a gauging job at Vaasa?
faqs.a: Not inside the ship. Holds and tanks are measured as at any other time, using a couplant that does not freeze and allowing for cold, condensation and the extra time needed to ventilate spaces. External shell readings alongside are limited when ice lies against the hull, and icebreaker delays can move arrival by a day or more. For scopes that depend on the outside of the hull, we suggest the summer.
